text: There are diverse views among scholars on whether future generations should be treated as rights holders under international human rights law.[[fn:68]] Most international standards do not explicitly elaborate on human rights in relation to future generations. At the same time, they do not expressly limit the protection of human rights to present generations. Due to a better recognition of planetary limits to economic development, States and policymakers for decades have been underscoring the importance of safeguarding the interests and needs of future generations.[[fn:69]] 69 The Declaration of the United Nations Conference on the Human Environment, of 1972, acknowledges that humanity “bears a solemn responsibility to protect and improve the environment for present and future generations” (principle 1). The famous definition of sustainable development – a development that “meets the needs of the present without compromising the ability of future generations to meet their own needs”[[fn:70]] – also illustrates the focus on future generations. One can see a continuation of this approach to safeguarding the needs of future generations in the 2030 Agenda.[[fn:71]]

footnotes.text: See, e.g., Stephen Humphreys, “Against future generations”, European Journal of International Law, vol. 33, No. 4 (November 2023); and the “EJIL: Debate!” in European Journal of International Law, vol. 34, No. 3 (August 2023), pp. 651–696.
Several declarations and conventions, as well as national constitutions, make a reference to future generations (A/68/322, paras. 33–38).
World Commission on Environment and Development, Our Common Future (1987), para. 27.
General Assembly resolution 70/1, preamble and paras. 18 and 53.

text: In addition to the concept of sustainable development, the principle of intergenerational equity has provided a basis to assert the stake of future generations in present-time decisions, as reflected in various standards clarifying or elaborating on the human rights of future generations. There is also a provision in the draft convention on the right to development requiring States parties to ensure that their decisions and actions do not compromise the ability of present and future generations to realize their right to development (art. 23 (b)).[[fn:72]] A. Rio Declaration and Vienna Declaration

footnotes.text: A/HRC/WG.2/23/2, annex.

text: Principle 3 of the Rio Declaration makes it clear that “the right to development must be fulfilled so as to equitably meet developmental and environmental needs of present and future generations”. This goal is reiterated in paragraph 11 of the Vienna Declaration.

In Agenda 21, adopted by the United Nations Conference on Environment and Development at the same time as the Rio Declaration, the Conference recommended that States adopt a national strategy on sustainable development, the goals of which should be “to ensure socially responsible economic development while protecting the resource base and the environment for the benefit of future generations”. The strategy “should be developed through the widest possible participation” (para. 8.7). The Conference also encouraged countries “to incorporate environmental costs in the decisions of producers and consumers” and “to reverse the tendency to treat the environment as a ‘free good’ and to pass these costs on … to future generations” (para. 8.31).

It is thus clear that both the rights and the needs of future generations have been on the minds of the drafters of international human rights standards for decades. Human rights have the unique virtue of being dynamic to adapt to new developments, situations and circumstances. In fact, the Vienna Declaration contemplates such an adaptation: “The World Conference on Human Rights recognizes the necessity for a continuing adaptation of the United Nations human rights machinery to the current and future needs in the promotion and protection of human rights” (part II, para. 17). 68 See, e.g., Stephen Humphreys, “Against future generations”, European Journal of International Law, vol. 33, No. 4 (November 2023); and the “EJIL: Debate!” in European Journal of International Law, vol. 34, No. 3 (August 2023), pp. 651–696. 69 Several declarations and conventions, as well as national constitutions, make a reference to future generations (A/68/322, paras. 33–38). 70 World Commission on Environment and Development, Our Common Future (1987), para. 27. 71 General Assembly resolution 70/1, preamble and paras. 18 and 53. 72 A/HRC/WG.2/23/2, annex. GE.24-12592 B. Declaration on the Responsibilities of the Present Generations Towards Future Generations

In 1997, the United Nations Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organization (UNESCO) adopted the Declaration on the Responsibilities of the Present Generations Towards Future Generations, which elaborates on various dimensions of the responsibilities of the present generation towards the needs and interests of future generations. Article 1 of the Declaration provides that “the present generations have the responsibility of ensuring that the needs and interests of present and future generations are fully safeguarded”. To achieve this intergenerational goal, “the present generations have the responsibility to bequeath to future generations an Earth which will not one day be irreversibly damaged by human activity” (art. 4). The present generations “should ensure that future generations are not exposed to pollution which may endanger their health or their existence itself” and “should preserve for future generations natural resources necessary for sustaining human life and for its development” (art. 5). C. Maastricht Principles on the Human Rights of Future Generations

The Maastricht Principles provide a detailed statement of the human rights of future generations. They find the legal basis of the human rights of future generations in: (a) international law not limiting human rights to present generations; (b) international law recognizing obligations and responsibilities towards future generations; and (c) other general principles of law, norms, customs and values recognizing obligations and responsibilities towards future generations (principle 2).

In addition to elaborating on intragenerational and intergenerational human rights obligations (principle 7), the Maastricht Principles outline the principle of international solidarity (principle 10). “Each generation must act as trustees of the Earth for future generations” and “this trusteeship must be carried out in harmony with all living beings and Nature” (principle 8). In “upholding the rights of future generations, States and non-state actors should draw inspiration and guidance from Indigenous Peoples’ knowledges, cultures and traditional practices” (principle 11).

The Maastricht Principles formulate the obligations of States to respect, protect and fulfil the human rights of future generations (principles 13–24) as well as the obligations, duties and responsibilities of other non-State actors, including business enterprises (principles 25–27). Importantly, they also include provisions for accountability and remedies for violations of the human rights of future generations (principles 28–36). D. Pact for the Future and the Declaration on Future Generations

States are currently negotiating a Pact for the Future for adoption at the Summit of the Future, to be held in September 2024. The aim is to annex the Declaration on Future Generations to the text of the Pact.[[fn:73]] In the second revision, the Pact contains a commitment on the part of the Heads of State and Government at the Summit to “conserve, restore and sustainably use our planet’s ecosystems and natural resources to support the health and wellbeing of present and future generations” (para. 26) and to ensure that decision-making today “takes greater account of the needs and interests of the generations to come” (para. 59).

footnotes.text: See https://www.un.org/en/summit-of-the-future/declaration-on-future-generations.

text: In the second revision of the Declaration on Future Generations, the Heads of State and Government recognize that the “decisions, actions and inactions of present generations have an intergenerational multiplier effect” and therefore resolve “to ensure that present generations act with responsibility towards safeguarding the needs and interests of future generations” (para. 6).74 73 See https://www.un.org/en/summit-of-the-future/declaration-on-future-generations. 74 See https://www.un.org/sites/un2.un.org/files/sotf-declaration-on-future-generations-rev2.pdf. GE.24-12592

In the draft Declaration, the Heads of State and Government commit to adhering to a set of guiding principles to “leave a better future for generations to come” and to fulfil their “commitment to meet the demands of the present in a way that safeguards the needs and interests of future generations”. These principles include maintaining international peace and security, promoting and protecting all human rights, achieving general equality, ensuring that future generations have the opportunity to thrive in prosperity and achieve sustainable development, ensuring a clean, healthy and sustainable environment, and building an effective multilateral system to enhance international solidarity and cooperation (paras. 12–21).

The draft Declaration also outlines several actions on the part of States. They include leveraging science, data, statistics and strategic foresight to ensure long-term thinking and planning; promoting the use of forward-looking impact assessments; taking a whole-ofgovernment approach to coordination on the development, assessment, implementation and evaluation of policies that safeguard the needs and interests of future generations; and fostering a future-oriented organizational culture that is mainstreamed across the United Nations system (paras. 34–41). VI. Taking seriously the human rights of future generations

Taking seriously the human rights of future generations – including the right to development – will require decision makers at the local, national, regional and international levels to identify and prevent as much as possible any adverse impacts of present-time decisions on the rights of future generations or on their ability to realize these rights. A failure to do so will “narrow the choices of future generations”[[fn:75]] and in turn undermine their ability to realize their human rights. For example, dumping toxic waste and dangerous substances, the excessive use of fertilizers and pesticides in agriculture, creating new technologies with racial or gender biases and the loss of biodiversity will undermine various human rights of future generations. The same could be said about prolonged wars and armed conflicts, excessive exploitation of natural resources, the extinction of certain species or the accumulation of unsustainable public debts. The use and testing of nuclear weapons similarly pose a serious threat to the human rights of future generations.[[fn:76]]

footnotes.text: Agenda 21, para. 33.4.
General Assembly resolution 78/240 and Human Rights Council resolution 51/35.

text: If humanity continued with the current pursuit of economic development and accumulative growth, little would be left for future generations on this planet to realize their human rights, including the four facets of the right to development: economic, social, cultural and political development. Article 7 of the Declaration on the Responsibilities of the Present Generations Towards Future Generations provides that “the present generations have the responsibility to identify, protect and safeguard the tangible and intangible cultural heritage and to transmit this common heritage to future generations”.

The collective dimension of the right to development will be especially relevant in the context of future generations, because many decisions taken by present generations concerning economic growth, infrastructure, city planning, the environment, trade, immigration and technologies will have an impact on future generations as a group. The Special Rapporteur recommends below four policy shifts to build an ecosystem supportive of the right to development and other human rights of future generations. A. Transitioning to the language of the “rights” of all “organisms”

With the exception of the Maastricht Principles, the policy commitments and standards referenced in the present report use the language of “needs” and “interests” in relation to future generations. Moreover, most existing standards tend to limit the concept of future generations to human beings. It will be desirable in the future to move away from both 75 Agenda 21, para. 33.4. 76 General Assembly resolution 78/240 and Human Rights Council resolution 51/35. GE.24-12592 these narrow positions: the language of rights should be used for future generations and the concept of future generations should include all organisms.

First, the terminology of rights confers a certain weight on claims made by the holders of such rights. It also imposes corresponding obligations on the relevant duty bearers as well as other actors interpreting rights (such as courts) or implementing rights (such as United Nations entities and development partners). Some stakeholders may be sceptical about using the language of rights for future generations because they do not yet exist and cannot exercise these rights. Suffice it to say that having rights is different from exercising and enforcing these rights.

Second, the language of rights would be helpful in situations where the rights of present generations and future generations come into conflict. In such scenarios, it will be critical to have a level playing field between the rights of present generations and the rights of future generations. It would still be necessary to strike a fair balance between competing rights. However, doing so should be possible by applying existing principles of human rights law such as proportionality and reasonableness.[[fn:77]]

footnotes.text: For example, “small gains for current generations should not be pursued when the actions are strongly likely to incur large losses for future generations” (A/68/322, para. 17).

text: Third, the concept of future generations should be interpreted in a broad sense to encompass not only human beings but also plants, animals and fungi. This is necessary because of the interdependence of humans with other organisms and nature generally. Adopting such an ecological approach will also be in line with the model of “planet-centred participatory development” proposed by the Special Rapporteur.[[fn:78]] B. Embedding intergenerational equity in decisions

The principle of intergenerational equity embodies “a concept of fairness among generations in the use and conservation of the environment and its natural resources”.[[fn:79]] While this principle is often invoked in relation to environmental justice or sustainable development, the concept of equity has broader dimensions and can be applied to all decisions taken by present generations with impacts for future generations.

footnotes.text: Weiss, “Intergenerational equity”, para. 1.

text: Decision makers – including governments and businesses – often plan for the future. Such planning is generally based on forecasted numbers and abstract future needs, rather than the human rights of future generations. To act in line with the principle of intergenerational equity, that must change. Article 5 (4) of the Declaration on the Responsibilities of the Present Generations Towards Future Generations provides that “the present generations should take into account possible consequences for future generations of major projects before these are carried out”. The foreseeability and severity of harm and the probability of its occurrence and irreversibility should be the key factors to consider.

The Special Rapporteur believes that social and environmental impact assessment processes should explicitly assess the impact of proposed projects on future generations and include specific steps to prevent and mitigate such adverse impacts. The same applies to human rights due diligence conducted by businesses, investors and multilateral development banks, in line with the Guiding Principles on Business and Human Rights. To illustrate, any project to approve deep-sea mining or hydropower must consider adverse impacts also on the human rights of future generations. Similarly, regulation of facial recognition technologies by Governments should include consideration of the impacts on the rights of future generations.[[fn:80]] Present generations should factor in how decisions concerning urban planning, biodiversity, automation, energy, infrastructure, trade, weapons, development finance and public debt will affect the rights of future generations. 77 For example, “small gains for current generations should not be pursued when the actions are strongly likely to incur large losses for future generations” (A/68/322, para. 17). 78 A/HRC/54/27, paras. 63–68. 79 Weiss, “Intergenerational equity”, para. 1. 80 Submission from Rita Matulionyte. See also Rita Matulionyte and Monika Zalnieriute, eds., The Cambridge Handbook of Facial Recognition in the Modern State (Cambridge University Press, 2024). GE.24-12592

footnotes.text: Submission from Rita Matulionyte. See also Rita Matulionyte and Monika Zalnieriute, eds., The Cambridge Handbook of Facial Recognition in the Modern State (Cambridge University Press, 2024).

text: Moreover, any impact assessment or due diligence process must integrate the precautionary principle in assessing risks to the rights of future generations, because where “there are threats of serious or irreversible damage, lack of full scientific certainty shall not be used as a reason for postponing cost-effective measures to prevent environmental degradation”.[[fn:81]] The International Tribunal for the Law of the Sea, in an advisory opinion, noted that “States must apply the precautionary approach in their exercise of due diligence to prevent, reduce and control marine pollution from anthropogenic [greenhouse gas] emissions”.[[fn:82]] C. Ensuring representation for meaningful participation

footnotes.text: Jose Felix Pinto-Bazurco, “The precautionary principle”, Still Only One Earth: Lessons from 50 years of UN sustainable development policy briefs (23 October 2020).

International Tribunal for the Law of the Sea, Request for an Advisory Opinion submitted by the Commission of Small Island States on Climate Change and International Law, Advisory Opinion, Case No. 31, 21 May 2024, para. 242.

text: Active, free and meaningful participation is a critical element of the right to development. However, future generations do not yet exist: “future generations do not vote; they have no political or financial power; they cannot challenge our decisions”.[[fn:83]] Yet, ways should be found to ensure their representation in decisions made by present generations, as nothing about future generations should be decided without them. In Agenda 21, the United Nations Conference on Environment and Development took note of the proposal to “appoint a guardian for future generations” (para. 38.45), while the Maastricht Principles recommend that “States must create accessible and inclusive bodies and institutions at all levels to ensure that the representatives of future generations can effectively participate in decision-making that affects their human rights” (principle 22 (d)). For now, children have been used as proxies in some cases to litigate for the rights of future generations.[[fn:84]]

footnotes.text: World Commission on Environment and Development, Our Common Future, para. 25.
Nolan, “Children and future generations”.

text: The Special Rapporteur believes that States and other actors such as United Nations entities, international financial institutions, multilateral development banks and businesses should create an enabling environment to facilitate the participation of future generations’ representatives. Such participation, which should assist in controlling risks to their rights,[[fn:85]] should take place at all levels and across the three organs of the government (the executive, the legislature and the judiciary). Several States such as Canada, Finland, Germany, Hungary and New Zealand have already established a variety of institutions to safeguard the rights of future generations.[[fn:86]] These practices should be mainstreamed and expanded. For example, Governments may appoint an ombudsperson or minister for future generations, while representatives of future generations may be nominated to join legislatures. Similarly, courts should grant organizations acting as guardians or trustees of future generations standing to challenge government policies and decisions or to file amicus briefs on behalf of future generations in suitable cases.

footnotes.text: Committee on Economic, Social and Cultural Rights, general comment No. 25 (2020), para. 56.
Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development, Governance for Youth, Trust and Intergenerational Justice: Fit for All Generations? (Paris, 2020), pp. 126–129.

text: The representation of future generations in decision-making mechanisms should be informed by an intersectional approach to capture differential and disproportionate impacts on them, because like present generations, future generations will not be homogeneous. Therefore, the present representatives of future generations should reflect diversity in terms of factors such as age, race, ethnicity, caste, gender, sexual orientation, ability, religion, socioeconomic condition, Indigeneity and migrant status. D. Reorienting financial planning and budgeting

Every attempt must be made to conserve and use sustainably existing natural resources. Yet, natural resources are finite and it is inevitable that future generations might not have 81 Jose Felix Pinto-Bazurco, “The precautionary principle”, Still Only One Earth: Lessons from 50 years of UN sustainable development policy briefs (23 October 2020). 82 International Tribunal for the Law of the Sea, Request for an Advisory Opinion submitted by the Commission of Small Island States on Climate Change and International Law, Advisory Opinion, Case No. 31, 21 May 2024, para. 242. 83 World Commission on Environment and Development, Our Common Future, para. 25. 84 Nolan, “Children and future generations”. 85 Committee on Economic, Social and Cultural Rights, general comment No. 25 (2020), para. 56. 86 Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development, Governance for Youth, Trust and Intergenerational Justice: Fit for All Generations? (Paris, 2020), pp. 126–129. GE.24-12592 access to some of these resources.[[fn:87]] 87 Therefore, present decision makers should reorient financial planning and budgeting to build the economic capability for future generations to realize their right to development. Countries may create a “future fund” in which a certain percentage of revenue generated from the exploitation of natural resources could be deposited and then invested responsibly. Such financial resources could then be used by future generations to build resilience and adapt to the new environment. For example, in Norway, the Government Pension Fund Global embodies a plan so that both current and future generations of Norway can benefit from oil wealth.[[fn:88]] While the establishment of this Fund was not rooted in protecting the human rights of future generations, this model can be adapted to embrace a rights-based approach to sustainable exploitation of natural resources.

footnotes.text: Depletion and/or degradation of resources for future generations are problems that the principle of intergenerational equity seeks to address. See Edith Brown Weiss, “Intergenerational equity in international law”, Proceedings of the Annual Meeting (American Society of International Law), vol. 81 (1987), pp. 127 and 128.
See https://www.nbim.no/en/the-fund/about-the-fund/.

text: The Special Rapporteur also recommends that Governments consult trustees or guardians of future generations for making decisions concerning annual budgets, fiscal policies and borrowing of money. There are existing laws or practices that could be mainstreamed to ensure that financial planning and budgeting takes into consideration the rights of future generations. For instance, section 2 (4) of the Australian Charter of Budget Honesty Act 1998 requires the Treasurer “to publicly release and table an intergenerational report at least once every 5 years”. The aim of such an intergenerational report is “to assess the long-term sustainability of current Government policies over the 40 years following the release of the report, including by taking account of the financial implications of demographic change” (sect. 21). The Government of Australia has periodically issued such reports, and in the 2023 report, it acknowledged how “technological and digital transformation” and “climate change and the net zero transformation” will shape the country’s future economic growth and economy.[[fn:89]] Such an existing process could be leveraged to consider the human rights of future generations and involve their representatives in developing an intergenerational report. VII. Conclusions and recommendations A. Conclusions

footnotes.text: See https://treasury.gov.au/intergenerational-report.

text: Despite increasing awareness about and evolution of standards on children’s human rights and child development, millions of children in all world regions continue to lack a dignified life and an environment to realize their capabilities. Children continue to face malnutrition, be trapped in poverty, be deprived of access to basic needs, be trafficked for sexual or economic exploitation, experience violence in multiple settings and be excluded from most decision-making processes. COVID-19, conflicts and climate change have exacerbated challenges for children to realize their human rights, including the right to development.

In the present report, the Special Rapporteur proposes that States and other actors should apply a right to development lens to realize all human rights of children in a holistic way. They should prioritize five action pillars to overcome ongoing challenges in realizing the right to development of children: investing in child development, nurturing responsible leadership, enabling participation, ensuring safety and facilitating remediation.

While children may be proximate to future generations, they should not be confused or conflated with future generations. Since the future of future generations is partly in the hands of present generations, they should not do anything to undermine the ability of future generations to realize their human rights, including the right to development. The Special Rapporteur recommends four policy shifts to build an 87 Depletion and/or degradation of resources for future generations are problems that the principle of intergenerational equity seeks to address. See Edith Brown Weiss, “Intergenerational equity in international law”, Proceedings of the Annual Meeting (American Society of International Law), vol. 81 (1987), pp. 127 and 128. 88 See https://www.nbim.no/en/the-fund/about-the-fund/. 89 See https://treasury.gov.au/intergenerational-report. GE.24-12592 ecosystem supportive of the human rights of future generations. First, the language of rights (not of needs or interests) should be used for future generations and the concept of future generations should refer to all organisms – not merely human beings – that will exist on the Earth in the future. Second, the principle of intergenerational equity should be embedded in impact assessment and human rights due diligence processes and the precautionary principle should be followed. Third, all present-time decision makers should create an enabling environment to facilitate the participation of future generations’ representatives in decision-making. Fourth, financial planning and budgeting should be reoriented to build the economic capability for future generations to realize their right to development. B. Recommendations

The Special Rapporteur recommends that States: (a) Allocate the maximum possible resources to realize the right to development of children – especially those from ethnic minorities or other marginalized groups – and to achieve all the Sustainable Development Goals; (b) Take effective measures to eliminate child labour, forced labour, child marriage, human trafficking and domestic and/or sexual violence involving children; (c) Strengthen institutions to prevent armed conflicts and wars and to hold accountable actors responsible for violations of children’s human rights during conflicts and wars; (d) Ensure active, free and meaningful participation of children and representatives of future generations in all policymaking and execution decisions, including those concerning the right to development, the Sustainable Development Goals, annual budgets, climate change, ocean governance, new technologies, trade and investment agreements and public debt; (e) Make available information to children about major policies, issues of national or international importance and development projects in an accessible and child-friendly manner; (f) Include children from diverse backgrounds in government delegations involved in multilateral negotiations for various human rights, environmental or climate issues and in regional and international forums relating to these issues or the Sustainable Development Goals; (g) Adopt laws and policies to ensure that child human rights defenders do not face any threats, bullying or intimidation for carrying out their legitimate work; (h) Establish child-responsive remedial mechanisms to address effectively violations of children’s human rights; (i) Establish an institutional mechanism, such as appointing an ombudsperson or a minister for future generations, to embed the principle of intergenerational equity in all government decisions; (j) Address the continuing adverse effects of nuclear legacies around the world to safeguard the human rights of future generations.

The Special Rapporteur recommends that businesses: (a) Pay a living wage and create a family-friendly work environment to enable parents and caregivers to fulfil their responsibilities to realize the right to development of their children; (b) Consult meaningfully children, child human rights defenders and child rights experts while conducting human rights due diligence; GE.24-12592 (c) Consider, as part of human rights due diligence or impact assessment processes, the adverse impact of their activities on the human rights of future generations and adopt the precautionary principle; (d) Ensure active, free and meaningful participation of children and representatives of future generations and consider intersectional impacts while developing new technologies and digital games; (e) Provide financial and other resources to organizations working on child development; (f) Adopt responsible advertising practices in relation to children and protect children and child human rights defenders from online bullying and harassment; (g) Establish child-responsive grievance mechanisms to handle complaints concerning violations of children’s human rights.

The Special Rapporteur recommends that multilateral development banks: (a) Conduct ex ante assessment of the impacts of project finance on the human rights of children and future generations and include suitable clauses in their contracts to prevent, mitigate and remediate such impacts; (b) Provide grants and increase long-term, low-interest financing for child development, especially to States under debt distress; (c) Ensure that their grievance mechanisms are child-responsive to handle complaints about violations of children’s human rights effectively.

The Special Rapporteur recommends that national human rights institutions: (a) Raise awareness about and promote the human rights of children and future generations, including by conducting public inquiries; (b) Constitute advisory committees comprising a diverse group of children to guide their human rights work; (c) Establish child-responsive remedial mechanisms to deal with violations of children’s human rights.

The Special Rapporteur recommends that the Secretary-General appoint a special envoy on future generations to ensure that the human rights of future generations are mainstreamed into the work of all United Nations entities and other international and regional organizations.

The Special Rapporteur recommends that international financial institutions adopt an intersectional approach in engaging children and representatives of future generations in their strategic policymaking, annual meetings and key decisions.

The Special Rapporteur recommends that educational institutions nurture responsible leadership skills among children and offer them education to inculcate respect for human rights, equality, diversity, democracy, peace and sustainability.

The Special Rapporteur recommends that school staff and childcare providers ensure the participation of children from diverse backgrounds in their decision-making processes and establish child-responsive grievance mechanisms to handle the grievances of children.

The right to development is the human right of every human person and all peoples to participate in, contribute to and enjoy economic, social, cultural and political development. However, due to persistent gender inequalities, patriarchal norms and structural barriers, women and girls, who comprise about half of the world’s population, are unable to realize their right to development.

In the present report, the Special Rapporteur focuses on the mutually reinforcing nexus between gender equality and the right to development. Without gender equality, the right to development cannot be realized, not only for girls and women, but for anyone, irrespective of their gender. At the same time, the realization of the right to development would lead to gender equality.

The elaboration of the nexus between gender equality and the right to development is pertinent for three reasons. First, the nexus between gender equality and the right to development has received very limited attention. In fact, the right to development is sometimes considered to be in opposition to the achievement of gender equality. The polarization between States championing gender equality and States promoting the right to development reflects that divide. It is important to overcome such misconceptions and underscore the nexus between the two.

Second, 2025 is an important year for gender equality because the world community is commemorating the thirtieth anniversary of the adoption of the Beijing Declaration and Platform for Action, a landmark document providing a blueprint for achieving substantive gender equality. Moreover, Sustainable Development Goal 5 on achieving gender equality and empowering all women and girls is set to be reviewed at the high-level political forum on sustainable development.

Third, in recent years, the backlash against gender equality has become more prominent, with attempts to roll back substantial gains made over the years.[[fn:1]] It is critical to reinforce the importance of gender equality as a cross-cutting foundational right that should not fluctuate with changes in the political winds. B. Objectives

footnotes.text: See A/HRC/56/51 and A/HRC/38/46.

text: In the present report, the Special Rapporteur seeks to achieve three main objectives. First, he describes the nexus between gender equality and the right to development. The enjoyment of gender equality by girls and women would lead to the realization of all four facets of their right to development: economic, social, cultural and political development. Conversely, realizing the right to development of girls and women would result in gender equality.

Second, he illustrates the ways in which ensuring gender equality for girls and women would have a ripple effect on realizing the right to development for all. In fact, when girls and women are enabled as agents of change, they contribute to a more inclusive, peaceful and sustainable world.

Third, the Special Rapporteur explains the ways in which various aspects of the right to development, including the collective dimension, participation in decision-making, fair distribution, international cooperation and intersectionality, should be leveraged to achieve substantive gender equality in society. 1 See A/HRC/56/51 and A/HRC/38/46. GE.25-11163 C. Methodology

In the report, Special Rapporteur builds on international standards on gender equality and the right to development. He also draws on relevant literature and the practices of States and other actors. His analysis and recommendations are informed by insights gained from engagement with many stakeholders over the years.

In response to the Special Rapporteur’s call for input, about 70 submissions were received from States and other stakeholders.[[fn:2]] 2 The Special Rapporteur also conducted in-person consultations in Geneva and Suva and organized four virtual consultations to engage representatives of various non-State actors from all world regions. In addition, he had bilateral conversations with representatives of the United Nations Entity for Gender Equality and the Empowerment of Women (UN-Women) and members of the Committee on the Elimination of Discrimination against Women and the Working Group on discrimination against women and girls. The Special Rapporteur is grateful to all stakeholders for providing input in various forms. D. Scope and limitations

footnotes.text: All submissions are available at https://www.ohchr.org/en/calls-for-input/2025/call-input-2025-reports.

text: In the report, the Special Rapporteur focuses on gender equality from the perspective of women and girls, applying an intersectional perspective. The focus on women and girls, however, is not meant to suggest that men and boys or non-binary persons do not face discrimination. Gender equality concerns every human being.

The Special Rapporteur acknowledges that, owing to space constraints, it was not possible to refer to all the international standards on gender equality or the right to development. Nor was it possible to examine all strands of the nexus between gender equality and the right to development. II. Selected normative standards concerning human rights and the right to development

As the brief review below shows, gender equality is a foundational and cross-cutting norm of most international normative standards on human rights and the right to development. A. International Bill of Human Rights

The Universal Declaration of Human Rights promotes gender equality. Several women played a critical role in ensuring that women were treated equally in the Declaration. Hansa Mehta is widely credited for replacing the phrase “all men are born free and equal” with “all human beings are born free and equal” in article[[fn:3]] 1.3 Article 2 makes that concept explicit, providing that “everyone is entitled to all the rights and freedoms set forth in this Declaration, without distinction of any kind, such as race, colour, sex, language, religion, political or other opinion, national or social origin, property, birth or other status.” The focus on equality is manifested throughout the Declaration, as most of its provisions use the term “everyone” or “no one” in reference to various human rights and freedoms.

footnotes.text: See https://www.ohchr.org/en/stories/2018/03/role-women-shaping-universal-declaration-human-rights.

text: The International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights and the International Covenant on Economic, Social and Cultural Rights strengthen further the foundations of gender equality. In addition to incorporating a non-discrimination clause in article 2, both Covenants expressly require States Parties to ensure the equal right of men and women to the enjoyment of all civil, political, social, economic and cultural rights (art. 3). That is reinforced 2 All submissions are available at https://www.ohchr.org/en/calls-for-input/2025/call-input-2025reports. 3 See https://www.ohchr.org/en/stories/2018/03/role-women-shaping-universal-declaration-humanrights. GE.25-11163 by the guarantee in the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights of equality before courts and tribunals (art. 14), the equality of rights and responsibilities of spouses as to marriage, during marriage and at its dissolution (art. 23), equal suffrage (art. 25) and equality before the law and the equal protection of the law (art. 26). The International Covenant on Economic, Social and Cultural Rights similarly guarantees equal remuneration for work of equal value (art. 7) and equal access to higher education to all (art. 13). B. Convention on the Elimination of All Forms of Discrimination against Women

The Convention on the Elimination of All Forms of Discrimination against Women marked a critical milestone in eliminating multifaceted discrimination against women. It defined discrimination in a broad sense to include “any distinction, exclusion or restriction made on the basis of sex which has the effect or purpose of impairing or nullifying the recognition, enjoyment or exercise by women, irrespective of their marital status, on a basis of equality of men and women, of human rights and fundamental freedoms in the political, economic, social, cultural, civil or any other field” (art. 1). Under article 2, States Parties agreed to embody the principle of the equality of men and women in their national constitutions or other appropriate legislation and to take all appropriate measures to eliminate discrimination against women by any non-State actors. Article 3 required States Parties to take all appropriate measures to ensure the full development and advancement of women in all fields, especially in the political, social, economic and cultural fields. The special focus on the development and advancement of women in those fields corresponded with the four facets of the right to development: economic, social, political and cultural development

The Convention acknowledged the role of temporary special measures in achieving substantive gender equality (art. 4) and the importance of modifying social and cultural customs or practices that are discriminatory to women or perpetuate stereotyped roles for men and women (art. 5). The Convention also contained specific provisions to eliminate discrimination against women in political and public life, to enable women to represent Governments at the international level and participate in the work of international organizations and to ensure equal rights with men in the fields of education, employment, healthcare, marriage and family relations and in concluding contracts and administering property.

Another key contribution of the Convention was its attention to safeguarding the sexual and reproductive health and rights of women, something that had not received adequate attention in generic human rights instruments. The Convention also introduced the intersectional dimension of discrimination, with article 14 focused on the specific problems faced by rural women. The Committee on the Elimination of Discrimination against Women has further elaborated on the transformative potential of the Convention in the achievement of gender equality through various general recommendations.[[fn:4]] For example, the Committee has underlined the importance of adopting an intersectional approach, given that discrimination against women and girls in all their diversity is inextricably linked to other factors that affect their lives.[[fn:5]] C. Beijing Declaration and Platform for Action

footnotes.text: See https://www.ohchr.org/en/treaty-bodies/cedaw/general-recommendations.
Committee on the Elimination of Discrimination against Women, general recommendation No. 35 (2017), para. 12.

text: The Beijing Declaration and Platform for Action, adopted at the Fourth World Conference on Women in September 1995, remains the most ambitious road map to achieving substantive gender equality. The Beijing Declaration reaffirms that women’s rights are human rights and encourages men to participate fully in all actions aiming towards equality. It also makes the connection between the advancement and empowerment of women and the goals of achieving peace, sustainable development and environmental justice. Moreover, the Beijing Declaration recognizes the need to mobilize resources at the national 4 See https://www.ohchr.org/en/treaty-bodies/cedaw/general-recommendations. 5 Committee on the Elimination of Discrimination against Women, general recommendation No. 35 (2017), para. 12. GE.25-11163 and international levels for the advancement of women, especially new and additional resources for developing countries.

Building on the Nairobi Forward-looking Strategies for the Advancement of Women and other normative developments, the Platform for Action lays down an agenda for women’s empowerment, including by “removing all the obstacles to women’s active participation in all spheres of public and private life through a full and equal share in economic, social, cultural and political decision-making” (para. 1). Twelve key areas in which urgent action is needed are identified in the Platform for Action: women and poverty; education and training of women; women and health; violence against women; women and armed conflict; women and the economy; women in power and decision-making; institutional mechanisms for the advancement of women; human rights of women; women and the media; women and the environment; and the girl-child. In addition to Governments, a role in all of those areas is envisaged for the international community, non-governmental organizations and the private sector. D. Women’s Empowerment Principles

The Women’s Empowerment Principles are a set of seven principles offering guidance to business on how to advance gender equality and women’s empowerment in the workplace, marketplace and community.[[fn:6]] Under the principles, businesses are expected to establish high-level corporate leadership, treat all women and men fairly at work without discrimination, ensure the health, safety and well-being of all employees, promote women’s education, training and professional development, implement supply chain and marketing practices that empower women and promote equality through community initiatives and advocacy.

footnotes.text: See https://www.weps.org/about.

text: The Principles provide targeted practical steps that businesses should take. However, considering the vital role of the private sector in all aspects of people’s lives and the global economy, businesses should not limit themselves to those action areas but should take gender-responsive and gender-transformative measures throughout their global operations.[[fn:7]] E. Declaration on the Right to Development

footnotes.text: See A/HRC/41/43.

text: The preamble of the Declaration on the Right to Development acknowledges the obligation of States under the Charter of the United Nations “to promote universal respect for and observance of human rights and fundamental freedoms for all without distinction of any kind, such as race, colour, sex, language, religion, political or other opinion, national or social origin, property, birth or other status”. As the right to development is a human right of “every human person and all peoples”, women and girls have that right both in an individual capacity and as a group and they “are entitled to participate in, contribute to and enjoy economic, social, cultural and political development” (art. 1). Participation in decision-making should be active, free and meaningful.

Since States have “the duty to formulate appropriate national development policies that aim at the constant improvement of the well-being of the entire population and of all individuals” (art. 2 (3)), such policies must not leave behind women and girls. That is reinforced by article 8, which provides that States should ensure “equality of opportunity for all in their access to basic resources, education, health services, food, housing, employment and the fair distribution of income”. States should also undertake effective measures “to ensure that women have an active role in the development process”. Considering that women and girls are disproportionately affected by conflicts and wars, the provision encouraging States to “promote the establishment, maintenance and strengthening of international peace and security” and to use the resources released by effective disarmament measures for comprehensive development is critical (art. 7). 6 See https://www.weps.org/about. 7 See A/HRC/41/43. GE.25-11163 F. Sustainable Development Goals

The 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development seeks “to achieve gender equality and the empowerment of all women and girls”; the aspiration is to create a “world in which every woman and girl enjoys full gender equality and all legal, social and economic barriers to their empowerment have been removed”.[[fn:8]] While Sustainable Development Goal 5 is focused on achieving gender equality and empowering all women and girls, gender equality should be seen as a cross-cutting thread running across all 17 Goals and 169 targets.

footnotes.text: General Assembly resolution 70/1, preamble and paras. 3, 8 and 20.

text: Sustainable Development Goal 5 envisages ending all forms of discrimination against all women and girls everywhere. That includes eliminating all forms of violence against all women and girls in the public and private spheres and all harmful practices, such as child, early and forced marriage and female genital mutilation. States and other actors should value unpaid care and domestic work. They should also ensure women’s full and effective participation and equal opportunities for leadership at all levels of decision-making in political, economic and public life. Equally important is ensuring universal access to sexual and reproductive health and reproductive rights, undertaking reforms to give women equal rights to economic resources and access to the ownership of and control over land and other forms of property and enhancing the use of enabling technology to promote the empowerment of women. G. The Pact for the Future

When adopting the Pact for the Future in September[[fn:9]] 2024, 9 Heads of State and Governments affirmed their commitment to accelerating efforts to achieve gender equality, women’s participation and the empowerment of all women and girls in all domains and to eliminate all forms of discrimination and violence against women and girls (para. 15). They also reaffirmed that gender equality and the empowerment of all women and girls was an essential prerequisite for sustainable development (para. 19).

footnotes.text: General Assembly resolution 79/1.

text: Action 8 of the Pact is focused on achieving gender equality because sustained, inclusive and equitable economic growth and sustainable development can only be realized when all women, adolescent girls and girls have their full human rights respected, protected and fulfilled. In the Pact, States agree to take “bold, ambitious, accelerated, just and transformative actions to ensure the full and equal enjoyment of all human rights and fundamental freedoms by all women and girls” and to “urgently remove all legal, social and economic barriers to achieve gender equality and ensure women’s full and effective participation and equal opportunities for leadership at all levels of decision-making in political, economic and public life”. They also agree to significantly increase investments to close the gender gap, including in the care and support economy, acknowledging the linkage between poverty and gender inequality.

The importance of achieving gender equality in relation to peace and security (action 19) is stressed as is science, technology and innovation (action 31). Gender equality is also an underpinning principle in the Global Digital Compact and the Declaration on Future Generations. III. Gender equality and the right to development

Despite a plethora of international normative standards and law and policies at the national level, achieving gender equality in practice remains a distant dream. A lack of gender equality is correlated directly with all four facets (economic, social, cultural and political) of the right to development. If girls and women do not enjoy substantive equality, their right to development cannot be realized.[[fn:10]] At the same time, the realization of the four facets of the right to development would contribute to achieving gender equality. Therefore, all States 8 General Assembly resolution 70/1, preamble and paras. 3, 8 and 20. 9 General Assembly resolution 79/1. 10 See submission from Biobele Danagogo. GE.25-11163 should embrace this mutually reinforcing nexus between gender equality and the right to development. A. Persistent and pervasive gender inequality

footnotes.text: See submission from Biobele Danagogo.

text: Girls and women continue to face various forms of discrimination in both the private and public spheres. A recent report by the World Bank revealed the shocking extent of legally mandated discrimination faced by women.[[fn:11]] Women enjoy less than two thirds of the legal rights available to men. Although 98 economies have enacted legislation mandating equal pay for women for work of equal value, only 35 economies have adopted enforcement mechanisms to address the pay gap. While 151 economies have laws in place prohibiting sexual harassment in the workplace, just 39 have laws prohibiting it in public spaces. In 62 economies, the age of retirement for women is lower than that of men. In 28 economies, a woman cannot pass her nationality on to her children in the same way as a man.

footnotes.text: World Bank, Women, Business and the Law 2024 (Washington D.C., 2024), p. ix.

text: According to The Gender Snapshot 2024, none of the targets of Sustainable Development Goal 5 have been met, with only targets 5.5.1 (women in local governments) and 5.6.2 (reproductive health laws) close to target. Those that are at a moderate distance to target include 5.1.1 (non-discriminatory legal frameworks), 5.2.1 (intimate partner violence), 5.3.1 (child marriage), 5.5.1 (women in national parliaments) and 5.5.2 (women in managerial positions), while goals that are far from target include 5.4.1 (unpaid domestic work), 5.6.1 (reproductive health decision-making) and 5.b.1 (women who own a mobile phone).[[fn:12]] The Global Gender Gap Report 2025 of the World Economic Forum reveals that gender-based industry segregation persists, with women still concentrated in lower-paying, people-centric industries.[[fn:13]]

It is estimated that it will take 300 years to end child marriage, 286 years to close gaps in legal protection and remove discriminatory laws, 140 years for women to be represented equally in positions of power and leadership in the workplace and 47 years to achieve equal representation in national parliaments.[[fn:18]]

text: Key barriers to persistent and pervasive gender equality include patriarchal social norms and cultural barriers, discrimination within the family, discriminatory laws, weak enforcement mechanisms, limited access to education, neglected sexual and reproductive health and rights of women and girls, the digital divide and poverty.[[fn:25]] 25 The coronavirus disease (COVID-19) pandemic also deepened existing gender inequality.[[fn:26]] B. Gender (in)equality and the four facets of the right to development

footnotes.text: See https://www.unwomen.org/en/news-stories/feature-story/2023/09/the-11-biggest-hurdles-for-womens-equality-by-2030.
See Paola Profeta, “Gender equality and the COVID-19 pandemic: labour market, family relationships and public policy”, Intereconomics: Review of European Economic Policy, vol. 56, No. 5 (2021).

text: There is a positive relationship between gender equality and the four facets of the right to development: economic, social, cultural and political development. Conversely, a lack of equality for girls and women will result in their non-enjoyment of those facets of development.

Economic development is not equal to the right to development, nor does the obsessive focus on increasing gross domestic product or pursuing cumulative economic growth ensure that development is inclusive. The Committee on Economic, Social and Cultural Rights recognized in 2009 that “economic growth has not, in itself, led to sustainable development, and individuals and groups of individuals continue to face socioeconomic inequality, often because of entrenched historical and contemporary forms of discrimination”.[[fn:27]]

footnotes.text: Committee on Economic, Social and Cultural Rights, general comment No. 20 (2009), para. 1.

text: Discrimination faced by girls and women has a direct negative impact on their economic development. It is estimated that, globally, less than 15 per cent of all landholders are women,[[fn:28]] including because laws in some countries do not allow them to own land. Even when women own land, they often lack decision-making power, as men typically control resource management.[[fn:29]] Many women face harassment in the workplace or public spaces and do not enjoy pay parity with men.[[fn:30]] Women entrepreneurs in conflict zones not only face gender-based discrimination but also the additional burdens imposed by sociopolitical instability.[[fn:31]] 31 Such exclusions and discrimination limit the economic development opportunities available to girls and women. The negative impact is not limited to women’s economic development, however. text: There is evidence that gender equality measures, such as gender-responsive budgeting, result directly in the economic empowerment of women and girls. Bosnia and Herzegovina reports that gender-responsive budgeting by the Ministry of Agriculture, Water Management and Forestry has led to significant increases in funding for rural women entrepreneurs.[[fn:33]] The Bolivarian Republic of Venezuela reports that its public budget law incorporates a gender approach, with resources allocated to such programmes as the Misión Hogares de la Patria, which benefits 3 million women living in poverty.[[fn:34]] The Democratic Republic of the Congo is promoting budgetary justice by prioritizing women and girls in funding allocated for essential expenses, including those relating to bodily autonomy, sexual and reproductive health, education, nutrition, housing, access roads and transport.[[fn:35]] 35 Gender-responsive universal health coverage policies would also ensure that girls and women enjoy equal economic development opportunities, because underinvestment in health can result in the shouldering by women of more unpaid care work, affecting their economic development opportunities.[[fn:36]]

See submission from World Health Organization (WHO).

text: Various countries are now taking proactive measures to use the positive linkage between gender equality and economic development. Ecuador reports that it promotes gender equality in the private sector through the Safe Company Seal, which certifies good business practices in terms of equal pay, work-life balance and the promotion of female leadership, while its National Agenda for Gender Equality 2021–2025 encourages State institutions to foster women’s access to credit, decent employment, social protection and land ownership.[[fn:37]] Colombia reports that its Ministry of Labour has implemented subsidies to bring young mothers into the workforce.[[fn:38]] Mexico reports that it has introduced several programmes to support women’s entrepreneurship, including the expansion of existing micro-, small and medium-sized enterprises owned or managed by women.39

text: In the Beijing Platform for Action, it is rightly recalled that, while accelerated economic growth is necessary for social development, it does not by itself improve the quality of life of the population (para. 14). Social development requires the centring of people in development decisions. It requires the adoption of a full life-cycle approach, ensuring the well-being of individuals and offering them access to opportunities so that they can realize their full potential. To realize their social development, girls and women should have access to basic needs, the freedom to participate in all walks of life and an opportunity to take decisions. They should also enjoy a life free from mental or physical violence.

Girls and women experience harassment and violence at home, in the workplace, in the community and in cyberspace. They deal with sexism and stereotypes and bear a disproportionate burden in terms of childcare. All of those discriminatory practices have a direct negative effect on their social development. States and other actors should take effective measures to combat such practices. Patriarchal social norms should be dismantled, including by engaging men and boys in gender equality campaigns.[[fn:40]] Legal reforms and economic incentives should be used to promote the raising of children as the shared responsibility of parents. 32 See submission from Elizka Relief Foundation. 33 See submission from Bosnia and Herzegovina. 34 See submission from the Bolivarian Republic of Venezuela (in Spanish). 35 See submission from Avenir Mère – Enfant (in French). 36 See submission from World Health Organization (WHO). 37 See submission from Ecuador (in Spanish). 38 See submission from Colombia (in Spanish). 39 See submission from Mexico (in Spanish). 40 See submission from Aline Ribeiro Pereira. text: Another aspect critical to the social development of women is sexual and reproductive health and rights, which are central to gender equality and to women’s human rights.[[fn:41]] To realize social development, women should enjoy autonomy over decisions concerning contraceptives, family planning and abortion and they should have access to comprehensive sexuality education to prevent adolescent pregnancies and gender-based violence and to make informed decisions about their sexual and reproductive health and rights. Benin, for example, reports that it has added a new category to its Act No. 2021-12 to allow the voluntary termination of pregnancy,[[fn:42]] while Honduras reports that its Plan for Equality and Gender Justice focuses on sexual health education.[[fn:43]]

footnotes.text: See A/HRC/47/38. See also submission from WHO and joint submission from Center for Reproductive Rights, International Lesbian, Gay, Bisexual, Trans and Intersex Association and International Planned Parenthood Federation.

text: Cultural development, rooted in language, the arts, religious beliefs and traditions, is an integral aspect of the right to development. In acknowledgement of the role of culture for sustainable development, peace and stability, the 2022 Declaration of the World Conference on Cultural Policies and Sustainable Development of the United Nations Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organization contains an affirmation of culture as a global public good and a call for its integration as a specific goal in its own right in the development agenda beyond[[fn:44]] 2030.44 Diversity in culture should be used to promote gender equality, rather than undermine it. States should not invoke cultural or religious values to deny freedoms, autonomy or agency to women, including on the basis of their sexual orientation or gender identity.

footnotes.text: See https://www.unesco.org/sites/default/files/medias/fichiers/2022/10/6.MONDIACULT_EN_ DRAFT%20FINAL%20DECLARATION_FINAL_1.pdf.

text: Due to continued discriminatory norms, girls and women face stereotyped depictions in advertising and the media, which undermines their cultural development. The fashion industry also perpetuates gendered social norms.[[fn:45]] 45 Considering the increasing role and influence of social media, States and companies should take proactive measures to curb the sexist representation of women in advertising, social media and film. Spain, for example, reports that its Women’s Image Observatory is empowered to take steps to deal with sexist and stereotypical depictions of girls and women in advertising and the media.[[fn:46]]

At the same time, many States are taking a variety of measures, including temporary special measures, to enhance the participation of women in political bodies at the national, provincial and local levels. Bosnia and Herzegovina reports that its Law on Gender Equality mandates at least 40 per cent representation for women in public and private bodies.[[fn:49]] Spain reports that its Organic Act 2/2024 is aimed at ensuring equal representation and a balanced presence of women and men in leadership and decision-making bodies.[[fn:50]] Benin reports that its electoral code was amended in 2019 to reserve 24 of the 109 deputy seats for women.[[fn:51]] Burundi reports that its 2015 Constitution ensures a minimum of 30 per cent representation of women in legislative, administrative and political organs.[[fn:52]] India reports that it amended its Constitution in 2023 to reserve one third of the total number of seats in the Lok Sabha (lower house of Parliament) and State legislative assemblies for women.[[fn:53]] The Democratic Republic of the Congo has waived candidacy fees for female candidates to encourage their representation in political leadership.[[fn:54]]

text: Such measures improve gender equality and assist women in securing political participation. To illustrate, because of a 2010 law in Senegal instituting absolute parity between men and women in elective institutions, women’s representation in the parliament had increased to 44.2 per cent by[[fn:55]] 2022.55

text: One should not, however, limit the political development of women to their representation in public bodies and institutions. Rather, political participation should be seen in a wider sense as encompassing all positions with decision-making roles affecting society, including in United Nations entities, multilateral bodies, companies, trade unions, civil society organizations and universities. It is a concern that, while women comprise about 67.2 per cent of the global health workforce, they remain significantly underrepresented in senior leadership roles.[[fn:56]] Mauritius reports that, to ensure a greater representation of women in corporate leadership, women must comprise a minimum of 25 per cent of the board members of listed companies.[[fn:57]] India reports that, under its Companies Act, 2013, all listed companies must have at least one woman on their board of directors.[[fn:58]] Similarly to companies, steps should be taken to increase women’s representation in the leadership of trade unions. Moreover, international financial institutions should aim to achieve the equal representation of women on their boards and in senior leadership.[[fn:59]] IV. Girls and women as agents of change

text: Gender equality is critical not merely for girls and women. Rather, gender equality is beneficial for all human beings. When girls and women are enabled as agents of change, they contribute to creating a more inclusive, peaceful and sustainable world. Various types of reforms can contribute to establishing such an enabling environment, including redressing disadvantages, addressing stereotyping, stigma, prejudice and violence, facilitating the voices and participation of women and girls and bringing about systemic or institutional change.[[fn:60]]

text: Below, the Special Rapporteur showcases the role of girls and women as agents of change in achieving inclusive growth, a peaceful world and sustainable economies. A. Inclusive growth

The current economic development model is leaving too many people behind. There is evidence suggesting that, if women are at the helm, they contribute to more inclusive growth. For example, women leaders in Rwanda have played a key role in ensuring inclusive growth, including through financial inclusion and by granting women the right to own and inherit property.[[fn:65]] 65 Inclusive governance in Rwanda, where women hold 64 per cent of parliamentary seats, has not only contributed to equitable development across sectors but also promoted stability and reduced corruption.[[fn:66]] 66 During the COVID-19 pandemic, women leaders spearheaded the adoption of more socially inclusive policies.[[fn:67]] 67 Similarly, women-owned businesses have been showing resilience in Ukraine during the ongoing war.[[fn:68]]

In 2015, it was reported that companies with the highest gender diversity in executive teams were 22 per cent more likely to outperform their less diverse peers in profitability and 67 per cent more likely to achieve superior value creation.[[fn:69]] Gender equality in the workplace would increase global gross domestic product by $28 trillion, or 26 per cent,[[fn:70]] including because of the increased productivity brought by women’s unique skills.[[fn:71]]

text: Militarization and conflicts in the world are related directly to masculine leadership. Evidence suggests that not only do women not generally start armed conflicts but they are also better at securing and sustaining peace.[[fn:74]] 74 Their participation in peace negotiations contributes to the quality and durability of peace, as recognized in Security Council resolution 1325 (2000).

footnotes.text: See Jana Krause, Werner Krause, and Piia Bränfors, “Women’s participation in peace negotiations and the durability of peace”, International Interactions, vol. 44, No. 6 (10 August 2018).

text: The 2016 Final Agreement for Ending the Conflict and Building a Stable and Lasting Peace of Colombia included a recognition of the disproportionate impact of armed conflict on women[[fn:75]] and gender parity provisions for the transitional justice system.[[fn:76]] Women also play a critical role in informal peace processes.[[fn:77]] The positive role of women in ensuring peace explains why 112 countries and territories have adopted national action plans on women, peace and security.[[fn:78]]

text: One major obstacle to peace is the current obsession with increasing military expenditure. The world military expenditure rose to $2,718 billion in 2024, a 9.4 per cent increase from[[fn:79]] 2023.79 More weapons do not necessarily result in more peace, however. Rather, weapons feed into war economics that survive on conflict. That is why article 7 of the Declaration on the Right to Development encourages States to promote international peace and security, including by achieving general and complete disarmament so that the resources released by effective disarmament measures can be used for comprehensive development, in particular that of developing countries. Girls and women can do more than they are currently to achieve that aspiration. C. Sustainable economies

text: Girls have been at the forefront of advocacy for effective climate action. Moreover, for centuries, Indigenous women have been the guardians of nature, aiming to preserve ecological harmony. They have been passing on traditional knowledge, including on saving and selecting seeds, cultivating and harvesting, to future generations,[[fn:84]] which is supporting climate change adaptation.[[fn:85]] Indigenous women in Guatemala and Mexico have been leading the revitalization of the milpa system, an Indigenous method of cultivation, which has increased the fertility of the soil, enabled the production of healthier crops and bolstered food security within the Indigenous community.[[fn:86]] Securing justice for the planet therefore requires girls and women to be at the centre of all economy-related decision-making, from development and agriculture to banking, finance, taxation, trade and investment.

text: The transition to clean cooking is another area in which women can provide critical leadership. An intersectional approach that involves women in the design and implementation of modern energy cooking programmes would contribute to the achievement of both gender equality and sustainable economies.[[fn:87]] V. Leveraging the right to development for gender equality

text: The Special Rapporteur has decoded the right to development to make its various aspects accessible.[[fn:88]] That human right has two dimensions (individual and collective), three elements (participation in, contribution to and enjoyment of that right), four facets (economic, social, cultural and political development) and five principles (fair distribution, intersectionality, intergenerational equity, self-determination and international cooperation).

footnotes.text: See https://www.ohchr.org/sites/default/files/documents/issues/development/sr/decoding-right-development.pdf.

text: One of the value additions of the right to development lies in its transformative nature, in that it requires economic and social reforms to eradicate all social injustices and establish a new international economic order rooted in equality and fairness. Therefore, States, United Nations entities, businesses, civil society organizations and other actors should use that transformative potential to address the root causes of gender inequality. Below, the Special Rapporteur discusses the ways in which five illustrative aspects of the right to development could be employed to achieve substantive gender equality: the collective dimension; active, free and meaningful participation; fair distribution; intersectionality; and international cooperation. As the figure below shows, each of those aspects is linked to various gender equality strategies. For example, gender-responsive public procurement would contribute to fair distribution and, in turn, would result in gender equality. Similarly, targeting development aid as part of international cooperation to address gender-based violence would result in gender equality by opening up social, economic and political opportunities for women and girls. 84 See https://www.iied.org/qa-why-indigenous-seed-saving-women-are-stewards-biodiversity. 85 See Jasmina Thomas and others, “Indigenous knowledge, gender and agriculture: a scoping review of gendered roles for food sustainability in Tonga, Samoa, Solomon Islands and Fiji”, Land, vol. 14, No. 6 (June 2025). 86 See https://hir.harvard.edu/resilient-roots-indigenous-agriculture-and-climate-change-in-latinamerica. 87 See submission from Modern Energy Cooking Services. 88 See https://www.ohchr.org/sites/default/files/documents/issues/development/sr/decoding-rightdevelopment.pdf. GE.25-11163 Transformative potential of the right to development to achieve gender equality A. Collective dimension of the right to development

Similarly to several other human rights, the right to development has both individual and collective dimensions. This collective dimension could be especially useful for girls and women in their efforts to build solidarity and focus collectively on human rights issues unique to their needs, such as menstruation, pregnancy and breastfeeding. The Beijing Platform for Action emphasizes that women share concerns that can be addressed only by working together towards the common goal of gender equality around the world (para. 3).

Collective advocacy by women and their organizations can be an especially powerful tool for reforming discriminatory laws and policies, patriarchal norms, social stereotypes and cultural values. Similarly, women’s organizations can represent the collective interests of girls and women in such forums as meetings of international or multilateral organizations or in due diligence and impact assessment processes conducted by States and companies.

Women’s organizations can also provide accessible and gender-responsive support to girls and women in response to gender-based violence. For example, Azerbaijan reports that it enacted a law on the prevention of domestic violence in 2010, has maintained a gender-based violence hotline since 2020 and is working on a new national action plan to tackle domestic violence.[[fn:89]] The Plurinational State of Bolivia reports that it has reinforced the guarantee to women of a life free from violence through prevention programmes at the national level and through the construction of welcome houses (refuges) and transitory 89 See submission from Azerbaijan. Active, free and meaningful participation

text: Active, free and meaningful participation in decision-making is a key element of the right to development. The participation of girls and women in all institutions at every level can be a powerful antidote to the discrimination, exclusion and violence to which they are subjected in both the private and public spheres. The Committee on the Elimination of Discrimination against Women, in its general recommendation No. 40 (2024) on the equal and inclusive representation of women in decision-making systems, provides a justification for why and a road map for how to achieve the equal representation of women. Girls and women do not require boys and men to empower them. Rather, they need opportunities and an enabling environment to participate in decision-making processes and institutions so that they can empower themselves.

The equal representation of women at the legislative and executive levels would accelerate the repeal or amending by States of laws that discriminate against women. Azerbaijan, Jordan, Malaysia, Oman, Sierra Leone and Uzbekistan, for example, have mandated equal pay for work of equal value or lifted restrictions on women’s ability to work in industrial or dangerous jobs. Cyprus, Malaysia, Oman, Rwanda, Sierra Leone, Slovakia and Togo have expanded maternity and paternity leave or prohibited the dismissal of pregnant women from the workplace. Armenia, Equatorial Guinea, Jordan, the Republic of Moldova and Suriname have enacted all together eight reforms prohibiting sexual harassment in the workplace.[[fn:93]] Saudi Arabia reports that it issued a royal decree in 2017 providing that no entity could require a woman to obtain a guardian’s approval to have access to services or to complete any administrative procedure.[[fn:94]] Other States should follow the examples above. It is also critical that legislation prohibiting discrimination cover both the private and public sectors.[[fn:95]]

For example, Mexico has conducted inclusive consultations on tailoring the implementation of the 2030 Agenda to the national context.[[fn:97]]

Girls and women should also be part of delegations negotiating multilateral agreements and participating in regional and international events organized by United Nations entities. A lack of female representation in decision-making structures results in inadequate healthcare policies and the persistent deprioritizing of sexual and reproductive health and rights.[[fn:98]]
